And so we have a dynamic team that works and is employed by the

Division of Early Childhood Education which is my division. The leadership coaches, they’re directly charged with providing coaching and support to the program school leader, and then we have instructional coordinators who work with the educators in the classroom and then social workers who really work with the school community and the families as well on all the things, programmatic, operational. Around– about your specific question, what we do all year-round is observe, assist and coach, and we tell our coaching based on what we need. We supplement that coaching, right, based on the needs of the children, the needs of the staff. Sometimes, you know, there’s a new teacher that comes in, they want a different types of support and guidance. And so what we also do is supplement with our Inclusion Specialist. And so this dynamic team, small but mighty, but they are growing. They actually go in and provide direct ways that we can ensure inclusive environments in the classroom. That is something that we want. We want to improve inclusion, but we also recognize that sometimes a child or little needs a little more specialized setting. And so that is where we work really closely with DIAL and the Bureua

of Early Intervention at the Health Department to make sure that we have coordinated services across, and that those coaches that I mentioned can really direct and tailor– further tailor their coaching for the staff based off of the learnings and expertise of our colleagues across the other divisions and agencies. I don’t know if you wanted to add anything?

I’ll just add that that the Committees on Preschool Special Education have a number of family resources including family guide about how to refer for evaluations to be considered for preschool special education services, and webinars including information specifically for families transitioning from early intention into preschool, and we’ll be sure to get this messaging out to all of the new 2K providers. In addition, we have a new role. Each of our 11 CPSE regional offices, thanks to the $70 million investment, it’s called the CPSE Director of Inclusion, and these directors are unlike regular CPSE administrators who have student caseloads and said they are there to support the entire CPSE office and all of the stakeholders that impact the family’s experience as

they go through our system. And so they will also be doing outreach and support in partnership with the inclusion specialist in Early Childhood directly to the new providers.
Great. And so it sounds like the approach that we’re taking now to 3K and beyond, we intend to continue with 2-Care as the new seats come online.
Correct.
Great. And again, I apologize if I’m duplicating here. Will 2K be full day, full year, as it’s currently being contemplated?

In the request for information that went out to providers, we aksed them to express their interest and capacity in both a full day, full year model, and also offer them the chance to express interest in a school day model. We want to understand the capacity that our providers have. We also want to understand family interest which we know varies by community– from community to community. So, we’ll be looking at that. We do anticipate many providers and families will want a whole day, but we have left open the option for both.
Got it. Is the 3K, Pre-K full day pilot getting any expansion? Is there a plan for that?
I’m so sorry, I’m not aware of a 3K, Pre-K full day pilot.
A parent– this is coming from an advocate. A full day pilot for existing 3K–
[interposing] Oh, the SDY+.
Yes.
Thank you.
With the additional funding for–
[interposing] Yes, yes. And so– sorry about.
No, no, please.

So, the SDY+ model is our extended day, but not extended year. We have grown to include– and let me give you the exact number, because I do want you to know. There’s 85 programs participating in SDY+ for those additional three hours and 40 minutes a day, and we have 2,855

children currently enrolled, and we’re hoping to increase that enrollment to 4,700. So, it is growing. They’re doing well, and we’re continuing to work with the participating programs.

And I’ll just close, Chair, very quickly by just saying, you know, we’re appreciative of the work and if there are legislative needs not contemplated by these bills that help achieve our clearly shared goal of expanding child care in New York City, I hope you’ll feel that you can work with us proactively. Thank you for your work.

Thank you, Chair, and good afternoon. I also want to just thank you for your patience in advance if I’m asking anything that has already been answered, or even if you just answered it while I was sitting here and I didn’t understand. So, I’m debating a third child. Just kidding. That is not why I’m asking. Just kidding. Listen, we have the first and the second. So, in seriousness, with respect to the wait list that we have for ACS vouchers of 16,000 interested families/children, do you understand that to be representative of the demand for that kind of child

care in the city? Can you remind me what the income threshold and requirements are for these ACS– existing ACS vouchers, and do we have shortfalls in this budget for the ACS vouchers? That’s number one. And just a related question, you may have answered it before, but as we do continue these conversations and want to get to universal child care in our city, how is the city assessing demand for 2-Care at this time?

So, I can start on your question about the Child Care Assistance program or vouchers. So, families have to meet a series of requirements to be eligible for those– for that service. They have to be at 85 percent or below of the state median income, have to have a reason for care which can be a work activity, an education activity. There’s a whole slew of others. And they need to– and the child has to be of legal immigration status. Families are also eligible for child care vouchers if they receive cash assistance, and there are a few other protected populations as well. So,families have to go through quite a detailed application process in order to be determined eligible for vouchers. So, we don’t necessarily view the voucher waiting list as representative of the

full population of families in the city who need access to care. We know the full population of families who need access to care is far, far wider than that, especially given the affordability crisis. We know families making many multiples of that still cannot afford care. Though, of course, we want to really focus on our lowest income families for whom the burden is greatest. At this time, the funding that we have from the state to support the Child Care Assistance Program is sufficient to meet the needs of families who currently receive vouchers and make sure they have continuity. We are continuing to talk with the state as we look at what it would take to serve a wider number of families who are on the wait list. And to your question about 2K, we are, you know, at this moment making some initial estimations of what we think demand might look like based on detailed population data, based on use of other child care services, but we also know we really need to get out into communities to ask families both in the places where we start and then citywide as we expand to really understand the full demand for 2K which we hope through outreach will also be able to reach a robust number of families.

Thank you. And then next question– I’m fairly certain this is what the Chair was asking when I walked in or shortly after– is around the mix of setting anticipated in this first year of 2K roll out– you know, our existing programs as you’ve said are in district schools and pre-k centers, family settings, things like that. For the thinking around the 2K expansion, what– do you have a sense of where you anticipate what kind of settings you anticipated the care will be provided at?
Yeah, for 2K we are looking at child care centers, community-based providers and others, and home-based providers. We are not looking at school-based programs at this time.
Got it. And then could that change in future years?

We’re going to continue– this is year one of the roll out, so we’re going to continue to look at how this goes and the initial community and what we hear from families and providers, but our focus as we expand to a younger population is really on our partners, our child care

providers and home-based providers who we know serve, you know, the city’s infant and toddlers today, and do it well and are experts in this, and we want to leverage their expertise and partnership.
And thank you. Just the last follow-up. Why are not– why are schools not being considered at this time for the past year?

As we think about the spaces that are most developmentally appropriate, healthy, safe for our youngest children, we know that that is most often our child care centers and our family child care providers. We also recognize on this rapid timeline to expand in time for the fall, we want to partner with those who are already operating programs for toddlers and we know can do it safely and well.

Got it. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much. Okay, sorry, I’m going to do rapid-fire, and then we want to move on to public testimony. Everyone’s been so patient. I had a question– DC Hawkins, maybe these are for you. They’re just

related to 3K and Pre-K. In the last budget cycle, a big push from the advocates and the council was really to stabilize the system, and we had spent every budget cycle really focusing on wanting to yes, fight for investments to 3K and Pre-K, but also just like understand. What– how– where are we in the process? And so I wanted to ask is there a target utilization rate for Pre-K and for 3K?

I know Council Member Restler asked a similar question, Chair, and so I want to work with AD Liss to make sure that we are aligned in whatever figure we come up with. So, we’ll get back to you on that one. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And then in the– I think it was last election– last election, excuse me– last application process there were a number of districts, school districts, one of which I share District 24 where there was a huge demand. In Queens there was a huge demand. What are you all thinking? I know these are things that you’re working on, but like, how are we moving seats? I know it’s not easy, but just tell me what that looks like, and especially in these districts where we saw a huge increase in applications and just not enough

seats where they needed to be, how are we going to rectify that in this administration?

Yeah, I appreciate that question. As part of the governor’s investments there were funds in there for the stabilization of 3K and also to add additional seats in communities that have unmet demand. And so as part of that expression of interest, we also included 3K for new providers to come into the fold or existing providers to add additional 3K seats— CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: [interposing] In the 2-Care–
[interposing] The RFI, yes. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay.

It is also inclusive of 3K. We also around the same time released two surveys, one for CBOs and one for family child care networks where they can express interests in modifying their slot configurations to better meet the needs of two-year-olds or three-year-olds for the upcoming school year. So we hope to leverage all three of those to improve the way in how we’re, you

know, providing care for three-year-olds across communities. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: And do you anticipate being able to make those modifications in the fall? Like, how early would you be able to take those responses and make those modifications?

We’re looking at those now alongside the applications. That was just in My Schools, the additional data that we’re going to get from the RFI to make determinations for the fall, but hopefully again, on the rolling basis, continue to look at it. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And then I just have a couple of rapid-fire questions on some of the data that you are able– just asking if you’re able to collect it. Does the DOE regularly review and analyze seat placement outcomes for 3K and Pre-K?
Seat placement outcomes as in filled seats? CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Filled seats and whether or not they were an applicant’s first, second, or third priority?

Oh, yes. So, we look at that data with our Office of Student

Enrollment who really manages our application data. They’re the ones who inform us on the family’s preference, and then also manages the wait list which a family could add themselves to even after the application period closes and throughout the year to maybe get a different choice based on their child needs. So, yes, we do analyze that data, and we’re using that to inform a lot of our thinking around placements in the future– placements. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: How often are you reviewing this data? Because it could move around.

So, the application data, we usually look at it right around the application cycle. So, now, right? The application cycle just closed, and we were actually looking at prior data to inform the application cycle in our conversations. We do look at it against utilization data on a monthly basis give or take, because it helps us, to your point, inform if– you know, why a seat might be vacant, if we need to move that seat, and then maybe connecting it to the admissions and the application data. So, I would say– don’t hold me to it, but I would say maybe a monthly by monthly basis.

CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. Excellent. And then if you can just say yes or no, the Department. Do you track match rates for first choices?
We do. We do monitor that. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: And what about outside– oh, I guess, they’re– plus top three choices at least?
We look at that as well. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, and then what about outside of their ranked preferences?
We look at that as well. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And would the Department be able to share the most recent numbers when you have it?

So, we’ll work with the Office of Student Enrollment to get that data for you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And then does the Department track wait list length and average wait time by seat type or geography?

So, I would have to confirm that with OC, but we will get back to you to confirm that. And the wait list kind of time you’re on a wait list can vary for a host of reasons, especially since you could be on multiple wait lists at one time. So, I’ll get a more robust answer to your question. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And I just had someone ask me this and I think I answered it correctly. The deadline was Friday, but if you missed that deadline what can you do?
You can add yourself to a wait list. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. At a family center or just on the– just on the website?

Any of a school program of your choice. If you are interested in attending a pre-K/3K program and you missed the application deadline, it is never too late. You could still go on My Schools, do your vetting. I always say pair that with New York City Child Connect which is the Health Department’s website, and then you can add yourself to as many wait lists as you want.

CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, I did answer that correctly.

You did. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Did not spread misinformation. Okay. And then I wanted to ask, regarding the 2-Care program that's currently funded by– it’s funded by the state, correct, per the investments made by Governor Hochul? Do you– and I think those seats are at 40,000 each for the 2-Care.
That’s the birth to two initiative. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Birth to two.
[inaudible] CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you for correcting me, and I don’t mean to interchange.
Of course, of course. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Do you anticipate investments from the city moving forward to expand the program, to stabilize the program in the future?

So, as we roll out for this first year, we’ll be working with all the agencies who have a piece to play, of course New

York City Public Schools, but the other agencies who will be supporting the roll out to assess whether we have what we need and we will certainly come back to you, and as we go through the budget process, identify where– if and where there may be other resource needs. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Excellent. And then just two final questions. So, regarding my bill, I think that there is– there’s obviously a lot of interest. We spent a lot of time today on 2-Care and quality education, but I think what is also kind of thrown around is universal child care, and I think for those folks that have been working on increasing accessibility for decades, their first question is like, well, who is this accessible for? Who is this affordable to, and who are you talking about? So, I would love to understand how the administration defines universality? Who are you looking to include, and is there– is there an interest right now with the 2-Care program to keep moving down to include, you know, zero to two in the same way?

So, universal to us means everyone. It means every child no matter their family’s income or immigration status or

occupation or zip code. Universal means everyone, and we believe that there are so many reasons why a universal system will more effectively meet the needs of all of our families, but in particular we know that as we expand we have to focus on families who are the least likely to participate in government services, because they lack the information or the language access or the time to find these programs. So we’re focused on expanding– as we expand to make sure we reach everyone, but to make sure that we are also offering really targeted support to the families who may have the hardest time otherwise finding these services. We also recognize that meeting all family’s needs will require a diverse array of child care options. Families have different work schedules and different preferences, and we want to honor and respect that. So, that’s a big piece of why it’s so important that we continue to talk with families as we go. The launch of 2K this fall is just the first step and it’s a really important step, but we know there is a lot more work we need to do to make sure we meet all families needs, including families with children under two, which we will continue to make

sure we’re paying attention to, and the goal is all children. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Absolutely. Well, thank you. I’m encouraged by that. It’s really important that when we are talking about universal child care that we remind everyone that we do mean everyone, regardless of your immigration status, of your income, and I know that for families in communities like mine, that is going to be really the difference between being able to afford to stay here or not. So I’m very grateful that those are kind of where the conversations are. I want to ask one last question, and I think you said yes, but just need the specifics. Just to– would you be able to commit that you could meet with the Council or brief the Council monthly on just updates, specifically about this expansion and this program?

We would be happy to. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, see? Okay, great. Okay. The last thing I will just say before heading into– it’s not a question– to public testimony is something that this committee is looking forward to working with you all and having a

discussion is also the realities of quality of care throughout the city. Council Member Sanchez was here and there were– you know, four years ago there were a couple– a few incidents where children were harmed and died. And I think that while we’re talking about expansion and the acceleration of all of this, I know that you all know this, but I don’t ever want to skip a beat when we are– you know, I wanted to give an opportunity to speak about children’s safety, provider safety every step of the way. So, please hold me accountable and I’ll do the same, but I just want to emphasize that, because I know– I think we can all get caught up on the excitement of how great this will be for the city, but we have loss children. Families have been impacted, and so I want to make sure that we are counting them, we are considering them, and that we are being mindful of the fact that it is not just a system that we can roll out from one day to the other, because we have to consider all of these things.

Yes, could not agree more. I think for us, making sure that children are healthy and safe, that parents have that confidence that their children are healthy safe. The

system does not work without it, and it is why we will hold all programs to an incredibly high rigorous level of health and safety, and I know that we need to make– as we discussed sort of earlier in the hearing, it’s important that we make it easier for providers to navigate those processes, but never– never with any compromise to the health and safety requirements they need to be. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Absolutely. Thank you. Thank you both. I know you said you’re going to–
[interposing] Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Oh, sorry.

No, I just wanted to say thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Yeah. I’m excited and I hope it doesn’t escape that it’s like– it’s two women doing this, amongst many other, but we’re all very excited. I now want to open up the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The

witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today’s hearings, please fill out an appearance slip with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today’s oversight topic and/or legislation. If you have written a statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at ARms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. First up, we have Grace Rauh, Donavan Swanson [sp?], Kellan Calder- my apologies- Jocelyn Mazurenza [sp?]- I’m so sorry– and Stamo Karalazarides Rosenberg. Please correct me. I’m so embarrassed. Hi, anybody can start. Two minutes.

Thank you. Thank you, Chair Gutiérrez. Wonderful to see you and to be here. Good

morning to you and to members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education. My name is Grace Rauh, and I serve as the Executive Director of Citizens Union which is home to the Five Borough Institute, a public policy program focused on tackling big challenges facing New York City. Let me begin by applauding the creation of this subcommittee. Establishing a dedicated body focused on Early Childhood Education sends a powerful and important message, that child care is not peripheral, it is foundational for the future of our city. 14 years ago when my oldest daughter was born, I was stunned by the cost of child care. I was working as a reporter at New York One. My husband was a law firm associate, and it felt like we had suddenly gone out and decided to rent second Manhattan apartment. That is how much money we were spending. Then, though, I saw the power of government to meet the needs of families. Universal Pre-K was a financial lifeline for our family and for thousands of others, and it showed that when New York sets big goals, we can deliver transformative results. Child care costs today are even higher. This is no longer just about individual families, but about whether our city

remains affordable, competitive, vibrant. At the Five Borough Institute, we have spent more than two years researching and engaging on this issue. Our major Child Care Policy Report identified structural barriers to affordability, workforce stability, seat expansion, and provided a policy roadmap to improve child care access and affordable. In October we convened more than 150 business, civic, and policy leaders at the first of its kind New York City Child Care Summit, and the message there was clear. The current system does not work for families, providers, or employers, and deeper public investments are necessary. Child care fundamentally is economic infrastructure. We know that this is an issue affecting anyone who cares about the future of our city. Fixing it requires broad coalition building, and we look forward to working with you and with others in the room to make universal child care a reality. We offer ourselves as a resource and a partner. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Grace. Thank you so much.

Hello. Good afternoon. Donavan Swanson representing the Office of the

Brooklyn Borough President. A lot was said today, so I’m going to try to be as quick as possible. Thank you Chair Gutiérrez and members of the Subcommittee for holding this hearing today and your steadfast leadership in advancing our Early Childhood Education. Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso remains a committed partner in prioritizing families and our youngest learners, and he supports many of the measures proposed here today to strengthen accountability, transparency, and the expansion of Early Childhood programs. The need for affordable, high-quality programs for New York City families continues to grow, yet we fall short in securing necessary seats to meet the demand. In Brooklyn alone, child care costs can represent up to 63 percent of families income. According to that same study, more than 80 percent of New York City families with children under five are unable to afford child care. Brooklyn’s child poverty rate is above 25 percent, highlighting the urgent need for accessible support for our youngest learners and their families. When families cannot access affordable child care, parents, particularly single parent households and female-led households, are forced out of the

workforce or into unstable employment, furthering economic inequality. A 2025 New York City Comptroller report notes that nearly half New York City mothers reported at least one child care-related work challenge, and 29 percent of New York City mothers and workforce reported dropping out due to child care concerns. By providing parents access to child care, we increase household income, level the playing field, and reduce economic inequality. This is not just about economics, however. Decades of research continue to support the overwhelming benefits of high-quality, Early Childhood Education programs and their relationship to student achievement and social/emotional development. I do want ot also note as this Council made us very aware, right, we also know that this conversation cannot happen without conversations around pay parity for our teachers, some of whom earn a starting wage of less than $36,000 a year. The same single woman-led household that struggled to access affordable child care also disproportionately represented in this same workforce. The system is just broken. It stacks the deck against those who need it most, our children, their families, and the educators caring for them.

So we must do right by our city. Borough President Reynoso stands alongside the Council and the Mayor supporting many of the steps proposed, whether it’s increasing reporting and accountability within New York City Public Schools, piloting programs that expand suitable locations for child care where real estate is scarce and expensive, and even expediting the child care permitting process, we must act to ensure that families have access to quality Early Childhood Education. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much.

Good afternoon everyone. Thank you so much for having this meeting. My name is Kellan Calder. I’m an organizer with New Yorkers United for Child Care. We’re a grassroots organization of parents, would-be parents fighting for free universal child care. I spend most of my days talking to parents on the phone, playgrounds, organizing WhatsApp, and the thing I hear most, that we all love the city so much, but we don’t know how much longer we can stay here or afford to be here. 3K and Pre-K it’s been a lifeline for these families, and one parent even said, 3K enabled her to go back

to work and stay out of debt, and these have worked, because they’ve been universal. So no means testing, open to every family regardless of income or immigration status. This universality makes them effective and trusted. And on the subject of effectiveness, I want to take a moment just to commend everyone who has been involved in the outreach efforts, because it’s been remarkable. The administration mounted the most aggressive enrollment outreach campaign we’ve seen since the early beginning of universal Pre-K. We received messages showing that the linkNYC ads are very effective, and it’s in multiple languages, as well as the personalized calls. So this sort of outreach isn’t just marketing, it’s trust building, and it’s something that had to be rebuilt which is a bit of why the enrollment has been an uphill climb because of the previous administration’s betrayal of faith these families had in the process and seats being cut. We know it won’t disappear over night and that parents need to know that there’s a city that has a promise for care, which brings me to 2-Care. So, the launch of free child care for two-year-olds, it’s a historic first step and time in the city, and we’re

thrilled to see it moving forward, but we encouraged by the seriousness with this roll out with the RFPs for new providers to focus on high-needs neighborhoods, the emphasis on home-based care, but we want to make sure it’s done right, and that starts with paying providers fairly. This is an important factor on whether this program succeeds or fails, and child care workers who earn poverty wages are not sustainable for building a universal system. So, it also means full day availability from the start, investing with the same level of outreach that we’ve seen for this 3K and Pre-K roll out, and maintaining trust with parents. This would be a high-quality program. We look forward to working with this council and this administration to make universal child care a reality for every family in the city. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you.

Okay. Good morning, Chairwoman and members of the Committee. My name is Jocelyn Mazurkiewicz. Don’t worry about the pronunciation of the last name. My dad joke is, how do you say that? Smith. It’s okay.

CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: No, but as a Gutiérrez, I’m so sorry that I disappointed you and your ancestors.

You did not. You did not disappoint me. My last name, I always say also, gives me like a leg up. Like in Kindergarten I had to learn the whole alphabet by just learning to spell my name. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Sweet.

Don’t worry about it. And I serve as the Assistant Director of the Facilitated Enrollment Child Care Programs at the Consortium for Worker Education, the workforce development arm of the New York City Central Labor Council. And as part of our mandate to provide a worker-centered approach to workforce development for over 20 years, our child care programs have connected working New Yorkers with streamlined access to affordable child care. Long before child care reached the national stage, we’ve been working to bridge the gap between policy and the classical needs of the workforce. We help families navigate the child care voucher system, train workers, support union child care funds like DC37 who [inaudible]

here. Shout out to Morgan Dolan [sp?]. Sorry– I’ve lost my spot. And conduct research on the impact of child care funding. Further, we lead the New York Union Child Care Coalition, a group of unions working together to address work/family balance and change the workplace to better reflect the needs of families. What we have learned from this work is that a truly universal system is not one in which every child has a seat, but one in which those seats meet diverse, ever-changing needs of every family, regular working hours for parents, accommodations for children with special needs, and child care deserts present challenges that must be addressed. Alongside members of the New York Union Child Care Coalition, we are actively working on solutions to close these gaps. To document the diversity of experience faced by working families, we have compiled stories of the individuals we serve into an interactive map which we would gladly share with the members of this committee. We are encouraged by the legislation. Basically, we’re looking forward to working with you. And we’re here as a resource, so call on us. We’re so excited.

CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much. The final–

Good afternoon, Chair Gutiérrez and members of the subcommittee. I’m Stamo Karalazarides Rosenberg. Also had to learn the alphabet when I learned my name. So, I understand that. And you actually pronounced it perfectly. Thank you. And I am the First Vice President of CSA, the Council of Supervisors and Administrators. Universal child care is not a seat expansion. Sorry. Universal child care is not a seat expansion challenge. It is a workforce and leadership stabilization challenge. CSA brings a unique vantage point to this issue. We represent principals, APs, and supervisory leaders across New York City, including Early Childhood directors and assistant directors in both DOE-operated and community-based organization. In fact, in 1976, CSA negotiated the first collective bargaining agreement for Early Childhood educators in the nation. Because we represent leaders across both delivery systems, DOE-operated and community-based, we see clearly where the structural misalignment is undermining stability. There are three issues that

must be addressed if universal child care is to succeed. First, pay parity. It is well-documented that educators and school leaders performing comparable work in DOE-run programs and community-based centers are paid on fundamentally different scales. These programs operate under the same standards. They serve the same children. They are part of the same publicly-funded system. Yet, one workforce is compensated far less.
